card.hook: Where else can you buy a bag of coffee, a bunch of flowers and a pair of snakeskin boots within about thirty steps? Welcome to San José Central Market, where every corner has a new scene and you'll want your phone out the whole time.
card.stand_here: Stand about 10 m east of the numbered pin, at the phone icon on the map, and face west. Then wander the nearest alleys and shoot along them instead of staying put.
card.zoom: Use zoom 0.5x for the narrow alleys and busy crossings, and zoom 1x for most stalls and people. Try zoom 2x or more (depending on your phone) for fruit, coffee or crafts, so you don't have to lean over the counter.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line an alley up with a vertical line, so the rows of stalls lead the eye into your shot.
card.best_time: Go when the market is open and busy, so the stalls are full. Expect crowds, and check a current map listing or ask locally for opening hours before you go.
card.selfie_here: Pick a colourful stall or a hand-painted sign and put it over your shoulder. Use the front camera, switch to zoom 0.5x to squeeze in more of the scene, and hold your phone high so the alley doesn't swallow you.
card.rules_and_safety: The alleys get crowded, so keep an eye on your belongings and your bag zipped. Ask vendors before taking close-up photos of them. Opening times and photo rules may change, so ask locally or check a current map listing.
card.challenge: Find a repeating pattern, like a row of stalls, strings of goods or stacked fruit, and shoot straight down it so it pulls the eye in.
card.good_to_know: San José Central Market opened in 1880 and is still a busy working place rather than a showpiece. It fills an entire block on Avenida Central, with more than 200 shops, stalls and small, inexpensive restaurants called sodas. If you want a second stop, Mercado Borbón, which specialises in food, is two blocks to the north.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand about 10 m east of the numbered pin, at the phone icon on the map, and face west. Then wander the nearest alleys and shoot along them instead of staying put.

selfie_research.safety: Keep an eye on your belongings, as the market can get busy and crowded (from Evendo's Central Market guide, https://evendo.com/locations/costa-rica/san-jose/attraction/central-market-san-jose).
selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a specific selfie spot or a passer-by spot with the market behind or the whole market in frame, so I have left both lists empty rather than guess. The pages describe the market's location: it occupies an entire block on Avenida Central between 6th and 8th streets, about 250 m northwest of Parque Central (Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Jos%C3%A9_Central_Market; Tico Times, https://ticotimes.net/2013/09/26/photo-story-what-you-can-buy-at-mercado-central). The Accidentally Wes Anderson page (https://accidentallywesanderson.com/places/central-market-2/) lists the market's coordinates as 9.935049, -84.08197, close to the position you supplied, and gives general composition tips (symmetrical framing), but names no vantage point. Photo guides say the market's entrances and facade are photogenic without naming a spot (https://airial.travel/attractions/costa-rica/san-jos%C3%A9/mercado-central-san-jos%C3%A9-OqWpTSQl). One related rule is not a selfie-stick rule: Mytourway (https://www.mytourway.com/destination/central-market-mercado-central/) advises asking vendors before taking close-up photos. No page I found mentions selfie sticks or tripods. The market is on Avenida Central, which pages describe as busy and crowded. To find real spots, you may need local walking-tour or photo-walk sources, or a check on the ground.

card.hook: Busy street, buses going by, and right in the middle of it all sits a big, solid cathedral that has seen the city change around it. Good news: you don't need to be a pro to make it look great.
card.stand_here: Find the phone icon on the map. It's about 25 m south of the Metropolitan Cathedral of San José, on Calle Central by Avenues 2 and 4. Stand there and face north.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to fit the whole front of the building. If you're too close or want more street in the shot, tap 0.5x. For the doorway or stonework, try 2x or 5x (depends on your phone), or just walk up and zoom rather than cropping later.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the cathedral's edges up with them, holding your phone level so the walls don't lean in.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer harsh shadows. Midday sun can be strong, so if the sky looks washed out, tap the cathedral and make the picture a bit darker.
card.selfie_here: Try Parque Central, at the big domed central pavilion in the plaza across from the cathedral. CNN calls it a popular selfie spot. Use the front camera at 0.5x, then check on the spot whether the cathedral fits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in Parque Central on the park side opposite the cathedral's main front, while you stand with the cathedral behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos inside are allowed without flash, but only when no services are on. Don't photograph parishioners without their permission, and men are asked to remove their hats inside.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot of the whole cathedral, then one close-up of a detail nobody else would notice, and see which one you like more.
card.good_to_know: The first cathedral on this spot was built in 1802, but an earthquake destroyed it. That's worth a line in your photo caption. Check the official site before you go if you want to look inside, as visiting arrangements may change.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Find the phone icon on the map. It's about 25 m south of the Metropolitan Cathedral of San José, on Calle Central by Avenues 2 and 4. Stand there and face north.

card.hook: Most museums make you squint at them from a narrow pavement. The Museo del Jade has a whole open square out front, so you can step back and get the entire building in one go.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, right in front of the museum on Plaza de la Democracia, and face the building. Then walk back across the plaza until the whole frontage sits comfortably in your frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x if you're close, so the whole frontage fits. Then go to 1x for a more natural look, and try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out details like the entrance or signs. At 0.5x the edges can stretch, so keep the building away from the corners.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines and line up the building's edges with the vertical lines so it doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Go in daylight, when the building is evenly lit. Quieter moments in the plaza give you a cleaner foreground, and if people wander through, just take a few frames and pick the best one.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the paved part of Plaza de la Democracia with your back to the museum, so the building fills the background. Use the front camera at 0.5x and hold it a little low to fit more in. It's not an official selfie spot, so shuffle left or right until the building looks neat behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Selfie sticks aren't allowed anywhere in the museum, and photos inside the galleries must be taken without flash. Photography inside can be limited, so check the museum's official site before you go if you want pictures of the displays.
card.challenge: Take a three-shot set: the full frontage from the plaza, a close-up of the entrance, and one texture or sign that catches your eye.
card.good_to_know: The museum was founded in 1977 by Fidel Tristán Castro, the first president of the INS. It moved to its current home in front of the plaza in 2014. It's described as holding the world's largest collection of American jade, which makes a great caption.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the phone icon on the map, right in front of the museum on Plaza de la Democracia, and face the building. Then walk back across the plaza until the whole frontage sits comfortably in your frame.

selfie_spots.why: Sources place the museum on the western edge of this plaza, so a visitor standing on the plaza would have the building behind them, but no page names it as a selfie spot.

card.hook: Imagine a country paying for its grandest theatre with a tax on coffee. That's the Teatro Nacional in San José, and it's worth a photo even if you never step inside.
card.stand_here: Head to the spot near Plaza Juan Mora. Stand about 25 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole façade in, since you're close to a big building. Switch to 1x for a more natural look, then try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for the statues and carved details.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines to keep the walls straight, then tap the brightest part of the façade and slide it a little darker so the stonework and sky both keep their detail.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the façade. For a night shot, switch on night mode and rest your elbows on something steady while it captures.
card.selfie_here: Climb the steps at the front of the theatre on Plaza de la Cultura and face the plaza, so the columned façade is behind you. Use the front camera (try 0.5x if your phone has it) and tilt up a little so the building fits over your shoulder. Golden hour is the one to aim for.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand out on the open Plaza de la Cultura facing the theatre's front while you pose on the steps, so the whole building fits in the frame (check it on arrival).
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is generally allowed in public areas during daytime visits, but flash is often restricted, so follow the posted rules inside. The plaza is described as well-lit with a noticeable police presence.
card.challenge: Spot the statues of Calderón de la Barca and Beethoven on the façade, then hunt down Chopin by the entrance walkway for a three-composer photo set.
card.good_to_know: The theatre opened on 21 October 1897 with Goethe's Faust and holds 1,140 people. It was paid for in part by a tax on coffee, then the country's main export. It's still a working venue, and its mural Allegory of Coffee and Bananas by Aleardo Villa also appears on the five colón bill.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head to the spot near Plaza Juan Mora. Stand about 25 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east.

card.hook: Let's be honest: the ground here is plain concrete, and nobody's coming for the paving. The fun is the people, the street life and a grand theatre sitting at the edge of it all.
card.stand_here: Stand on the steps in front of the Teatro Nacional and face out over the plaza. The theatre's neoclassical facade fills your foreground, and the open square and its visitors spread out behind it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole facade and plaza in one frame. Switch to 1x for a cleaner, less stretched look at the theatre, and try 2x (if your phone has it) for people and small scenes across the square.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and hold your phone level so the facade's vertical lines stay straight and the building doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Golden hour at the theatre steps is the one a travel blog recommends. Go at a quieter, off-peak time for a clear view of the facade, or pick a busy moment if you want people in your picture.
card.selfie_here: Try the steps in front of the Teatro Nacional, ideally at golden hour: front camera, zoom 0.5x, and check the plaza is behind you before you tap. For something different, find the glass panels set into the paving, where the underground Gold Museum is visible, and play with the reflections.
card.rules_and_safety: Several reviewers advise keeping an eye on your belongings because of petty crime, particularly after dark.
card.challenge: Catch one candid moment: a stranger crossing the plaza with the theatre rising behind them.
card.good_to_know: The plaza sits between Avenida Central and Avenida Segunda, between calles 3 and 5, with the Teatro Nacional on its edge. For a second view, walk out into the plaza and look back at the theatre, or shoot from the Avenida Central entrance for a street-level scene. Reviews say it gets crowded at weekends and at peak hours.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the steps in front of the Teatro Nacional and face out over the plaza. The theatre's neoclassical facade fills your foreground, and the open square and its visitors spread out behind it.

card.hook: Most wildlife photos start with a lot of chasing. Here, the butterflies settle on flowers right beside you, so the trick is to stand still and wait.
card.stand_here: Go inside and stand among the flowering plants near the waterfall area, where the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Face the flowers, with the waterfall and glass walls behind them.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for flowers, butterflies and the waterfall. Go to 0.5x to fit the whole waterfall scene in, and try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for butterflies that land out of reach.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the butterfly, then slide the brightness down a touch so pale wings don't wash out.
card.best_time: Bright daytime hours suit butterflies, and a quieter visit makes framing easier. Opening hours vary between listings, so check the official site before you go.
card.selfie_here: Try the garden's entrance, where visitors do take photos. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x, and hold the phone a little low so the gate and the green frontage fit over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: It's a paid garden, so check the official site for admission and any photography rules or fees. The trail down toward the river is steep and can be slippery, so wear good shoes.
card.challenge: Find all three stars (the blue Morpho, an owl butterfly and the zebra heliconian) and get each one sitting on a flower.
card.good_to_know: Spirogyra is a small butterfly house in Barrio Amón, just north of Zoológico Simón Bolívar. Roughly 50 to 60 species of Costa Rican butterflies fly around inside, along with a few free-flying birds. There's also a learning centre where you can watch caterpillars feeding on their host plants.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Go inside and stand among the flowering plants near the waterfall area, where the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Face the flowers, with the waterfall and glass walls behind them.

No page states rules on selfie sticks or tripods. I could not confirm that the coordinates 9.94005, -84.07275 match the garden: sources place it variously in Guadalupe (150 m south of El Pueblo), Barrio Amón (Calle 4), Barrio Tournón, and Goicoechea (Ruta 108, Calle 11). Opening hours also conflict: costarica.com lists 8 a.m. to 4 p.m., while the official site lists Friday to Sunday 9 a.m. to 1 p.m. and Monday to Thursday 9 a.m. to 2 p.m. Check before visiting.

card.hook: Picture a huge green lawn, a few big trees, and a jogger crossing the scene while a stadium waits in the distance. That's La Sabana, and it's a nice break from street photos.
card.stand_here: Head to the phone icon near Calle 48, about 410 m north-east of the subject, and face south-west. Stay out on the open grass so the whole building fits in your frame.
card.zoom: Start at 0.5x for the lawns and big sky, then switch to 1x for a natural look at buildings and people. Try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the stadium or a runner on the track.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the horizon on the top or bottom third line, and use a tree or path in front to add depth.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon gives softer light and gentler shadows on the grass. Midday sun is bright and a bit flat.
card.selfie_here: Try the paved path along the artificial lake, with the water and the National Stadium behind you. Use the front camera at 0.5x, hold it a little low, and let the stadium sit over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: For a bigger backdrop, ask someone on the Hilton hotel's terrace bar to take your photo while you stand at the terrace edge, with the park and stadium below you (check the Hilton's exact spot on the map first).
card.rules_and_safety: The lake path can be bumpy, so watch your footing while you line up a shot. The museum and stadium may have their own access rules, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Catch a jogger or skater as a tiny figure on the big green lawn, with a building behind them.
card.good_to_know: La Sabana is the largest urban park in Costa Rica, often called "the lungs of San José". It was officially inaugurated in 1977, though people have used the land for recreation for about two centuries. The Costa Rican Museum of Art is in the former main building of the old La Sabana Airport, and the park was declared National Architectural Heritage in 2001.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head to the phone icon near Calle 48, about 410 m north-east of the subject, and face south-west. Stay out on the open grass so the whole building fits in your frame.

card.hook: Plot twist: this art museum used to be an airport. The long, low building you're looking at was La Sabana's terminal, and now the only things taking off are your holiday photos.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the subject, where the phone icon sits at the Costa Rican Museum of Art, and face south for the main view. Then walk back across the park until the whole building fits in your frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x when you're close, because the building is about 67 m across. Switch to 1x for a more natural look, then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for the entrance or a façade detail.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines and line them up with the roofline so the long horizontals stay straight.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the façade than midday. Check the museum's opening days before you go.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the forecourt in front of the main façade, with the old terminal behind you. Or head round the back to the sculpture garden, near Jorge Jiménez Deredia's 'Imagen Cósmica', and put the museum's back wall behind you. Use the front camera, or try 0.5x so more building squeezes in over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the sidewalk at the corner of Calle 42 and Paseo Colón, facing the front of the building, while you stand in front of the façade so the whole thing fits in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Skip the flash, as a travel guide says it can damage artworks. Photo rules inside can differ from outside, so ask staff before you shoot in the galleries. The park grounds are public, but the museum itself may be ticketed or restricted, so check the official site first.
card.challenge: Take three frames: the whole building, a close-up of the entrance, and one with park greenery in the foreground, then pick your favourite.
card.good_to_know: Building began in 1937 and the terminal opened in 1940. After the airport closed in 1974, the old terminal became an art museum, opening on 3 May 1978. It was named architectural heritage of Costa Rica in 1986 and reopened in October 2011 after a renovation.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at the subject, where the phone icon sits at the Costa Rican Museum of Art, and face south for the main view. Then walk back across the park until the whole building fits in your frame.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found states rules about selfie sticks or tripods, so none are reported. The ask-someone spot is the Calle 42 and Paseo Colón corner named as the museum's address; the framing advice is my own inference, not from a source. The sources disagree on opening hours (one says Tuesday to Sunday 9am to 4pm, another Tuesday to Saturday 10am to 4pm), so I left hours out. card.hook: A butter-yellow fortress with turrets, sitting right next to a city plaza, and it's actually a museum. It looks like it should be guarding a pirate treasure, and the open sky around it makes it a great phone photo.
card.stand_here: Stand in Plaza de la Democracia y de la Abolición del Ejército, across the plaza from the museum's west facade. Face the museum so the yellow walls, the turrets and the tiered concrete steps are all in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the whole facade in. Try zoom 0.5x if you want the steps and statues big in the foreground, but keep the building's edges away from the corners of the frame so it doesn't stretch. Then zoom 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for the turrets and windows.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, hold your phone level so the walls stay straight, then tap the yellow wall and slide it a little darker if the sky looks washed out.
card.best_time: Late afternoon is likely to be best, because the west-facing facade gets softer, warmer light on the yellow walls. Mornings can leave it in shade.
card.selfie_here: Try the stone sphere circle on the plaza, just outside the museum. Use the front camera, hold it a little above eye level, and step back so you get more than just the sphere in the shot. For a different backdrop, the museum's inner courtyard has the stone spheres collection and good city views, though I haven't seen anyone report a selfie there.
card.ask_someone: Stand on the plaza across from the museum's front and ask a passer-by to frame the fortress-style building behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photo rules inside can change, and reports differ on whether indoor photos are allowed, so check the signs in each gallery or ask at the entrance. Keep a respectful distance from exhibits.
card.challenge: Wait for a statue to wander into one side of your frame, then get it and the tallest turret in the same shot.
card.good_to_know: The building went up in 1917 as the Bellavista barracks and housed soldiers. It was caught up in the Costa Rican Civil War of 1948, and the museum moved in in 1950. Inside you'll find historical documents and national treasures, but the pre-Columbian room has been reported closed for remodelling, so check before you go if that's why you're visiting.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Plaza de la Democracia y de la Abolición del Ejército, across the plaza from the museum's west facade. Face the museum so the yellow walls, the turrets and the tiered concrete steps are all in front of you.

card.hook: Here's the twist: you're standing in an ordinary open square, and the gold museum is hidden right under your feet. There's no grand building to shoot, so this photo is all about the secret below.
card.stand_here: Head for the Plaza de la Cultura in San José and stand right at the phone icon on the map, which marks the spot. Take your first photo there, then step back a few paces so the open square and some sky fit in.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for a natural view of the plaza. Switch to 0.5x to squeeze in more of the square and sky, or try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out people crossing the plaza.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and keep your phone level so the buildings don't lean, then put the sky or the plaza on a third line, whichever looks better that day.
card.best_time: Pick a quieter moment so you get clear space in the foreground, and go for soft daylight rather than harsh midday sun. Take a few frames at different times, because the square changes with the crowds.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the plaza's glass panels, which show the underground museum below, and hold your phone at the front camera with zoom 0.5x so the square fits behind you. Or stand at the museum's entrance on the plaza and keep it over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: If you plan to go inside, check the official site first for the rules on taking photos in the galleries.
card.challenge: Wait for a gap in the crowd and catch one person walking across the empty plaza, so your photo says 'museum hiding underneath' with a bit of scale.
card.good_to_know: The museum belongs to the Banco Central de Costa Rica and holds 3,567 Pre-Columbian objects, including 1,586 gold pieces dating from around 300 to 400 BC up to 1550 AD. Inside you'll find small gold frogs, eagles and jaguars, plus a life-size gold warrior in a glass case. The same building also has a coin museum, which includes Costa Rica's first coin, minted in 1825.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for the Plaza de la Cultura in San José and stand right at the phone icon on the map, which marks the spot. Take your first photo there, then step back a few paces so the open square and some sky fit in.

No selfie-stick or tripod rules and no safety point were found on any page.

card.hook: Here's a square that tells you where you are without a single sign: a big open plaza, a giant stone sphere on one side, and the building where Costa Rica's lawmakers meet right in front of you. Hello, capital city.
card.stand_here: Stand at the front of the Museo Nacional de Costa Rica, facing across the plaza. From there the middle of the plaza lies to the west, about 1 minute on foot.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x so the whole plaza, both sides and the Jade Museum all fit in one frame. If the edges look stretched, switch to 1x and try panorama mode.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the building edges up with them so nothing leans.
card.best_time: Late afternoon gives softer light and gentler shadows on the buildings. Stick to daytime and head off before dark.
card.selfie_here: Head up to the raised terraces of the plaza, where you can get the city skyline and mountains behind you. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and hold it a little low so the view fits over your shoulder. The sphere structure at the National Museum entrance is a fun second backdrop.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand in front of the National Museum, near the sphere enclosure at the main entrance and facing the plaza, while you pose out in the open square so they can fit the whole place in.
card.rules_and_safety: One guide advises avoiding San José's parks and public spaces after dark, so go in daylight and don't linger with your phone out once it gets dark. The museums beside the plaza may have their own opening times and entry rules, so check their official sites. The Figueres monument was reported as ordered removed, so check it's still there before you plan your shot around it.
card.challenge: Wait for a stranger to stroll across the middle of the paved space, then snap them so the plaza looks as huge as it feels.
card.good_to_know: The plaza opened in 1989 to mark 100 years since President Bernardo Soto Alfaro stepped aside rather than fight violently over his defeat in the 1889 election. In 2016 it took a longer name that also remembers the abolition of the army. That happened in 1948, and it happened right here.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the front of the Museo Nacional de Costa Rica, facing across the plaza. From there the middle of the plaza lies to the west, about 1 minute on foot.

selfie_spots.why: The concrete plaza has some elevated terraces which allow views of the skyline and mountains surrounding the city. Especially beautiful at sunset.

selfie_research.notes: The Don Pepe (Figueres) bronze monument, a common photo subject in the plaza, was ordered removed indefinitely by the government in a recent report (Semanario Universidad), so it was not used as a spot; check before going. The Tripadvisor and visitor pages found do not describe a specific selfie angle, so the spots are inferred from the terraces and sphere layout described there. The ask-someone position is an inference from these descriptions, not a page's photo tip. No page gave selfie stick or tripod rules.

card.hook: Picture a leafy green tunnel with a little domed bandstand glowing at the far end. That's the Paseo de las Damas, and it frames your photo before you've even lifted your phone.
card.stand_here: Stand on the Paseo de las Damas, coming in from the south along the avenue that leads to Parque Morazán, and face along the path toward the Templo de la Música at the end.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the walkway and the Music Temple together. Switch to zoom 0.5x to catch the full canopy of branches overhead. Try zoom 2x or higher (depending on your phone) to pull the bandstand closer and squash the path together.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines to keep the path centred, then tap the Music Temple and slide the brightness a little darker if the bright gap at the end of the path washes out.
card.best_time: Go in the morning or late afternoon, when the sun isn't straight overhead and the light under the trees is softer. A quieter moment also helps keep the path clear.
card.selfie_here: Head to the entrance and stand in front of the pair of golden wings (the Golden Wings of Mexico sculpture). Use the front camera at 0.5x if your phone has it, hold it a little low, and let the wings fill the space behind your shoulders. Check the framing on the spot.
card.rules_and_safety: Be cautious about panhandlers and consider visiting in daylight. It's a public park, so check the official site for closures or photo restrictions before you go.
card.challenge: Take three shots of the path: one at chest height, one down low to make it look longer, and one where a single walker in the distance gives it scale. Which one wins?
card.good_to_know: Parque Morazán is a city park in San José, shaded by large trees. At its centre is the Templo de la Música, a neoclassical bandstand with columns and a dome. On the Paseo de las Damas, the dama trees meet overhead to form a leafy canopy.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the Paseo de las Damas, coming in from the south along the avenue that leads to Parque Morazán, and face along the path toward the Templo de la Música at the end. The phone icon doesn't sit on this avenue, so use the map to find the path first.

The Temple of Music (the park's central gazebo) and the peace garden with a tiered fountain are named by sources, but no page describes them as a photo spot or gives a vantage point, so I did not list them. Its panhandler advice is also the only safety point I used.

card.hook: Picture a huge curved roof sitting in the middle of a big green park, with nothing in the way. That's the National Stadium, and it's one of the easiest buildings in San José to fit in a photo.
card.stand_here: Go to the phone icon near Calle 62A, about 55 m north of the subject, and face south. The whole stadium sits in front of you with open ground in between.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the stadium with a bit of sky and park around it. If you end up close and the roof gets cut off, tap zoom 0.5x. Then try zoom 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for the roofline and the big video screen.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the base of the stadium on the lower line and keep your phone level so the curved roof doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light, with fewer harsh shadows on the roof than at midday. Pick a quiet day if you'd like the park to yourself, because match and concert days can be busy.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera and tap zoom 0.5x so the stadium fits behind you, then hold the phone a little high and a bit to one side so the roof shows over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Along the lakeside stretch of the La Sabana Park External Circuit, the paved path has views of the stadium across the water, so hand your phone to a passer-by and ask them to frame you from the lakeshore path with the stadium behind you (check on the spot that it all fits).
card.rules_and_safety: The stadium stands in a public park, but getting inside depends on events, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take three frames at different distances, keep the horizon dead level in all of them, and see which one you like best. Bonus points if a person walking through the park gives you a sense of scale.
card.good_to_know: The stadium was completed in early 2011 and opened to the public on 26 March that year. It holds around 42,000 seats and is home to the national football team. China financed and built it, and about 800 Chinese workers came over for the job, which makes a good caption. It was the first modern sporting and events arena built in Central America, and it replaced the old National Stadium, which was demolished in 2008.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Go to the phone icon near Calle 62A, about 55 m north of the subject, and face south. The whole stadium sits in front of you with open ground in between.

ask_someone_spot.detail: On the paved circuit that runs beside the artificial lake in La Sabana park; the source says this route has views of the National Stadium across the water. It does not name an exact photo position, so the passer-by should stand along the lakeshore path and frame the stadium from there.
